title: Installation
content: The package is organized like this:
Drop the whole folder into your project (e.g. under `Assets/` or `Packages/`). If you're using Unity's Package Manager with a local/git package, point it at the folder containing these subfolders.
There's nothing to configure and no setup wizard. Once the scripts are in your project, the package is ready to use.

title: Initial Setup
content: There is no manager object you need to place in your scene to start saving and loading data. The core system, `SimpleSaveLoad`, is a static class and it's always available, from any script, the moment the package is imported.
The only thing you can place in a scene is the optional `AutoSaveManager` component, covered later in this guide.

That's the whole mental model in two lines: `SetData` writes something under a name, `GetData` reads it back. Everything else in this guide is refinement on top of that idea.

title: Basic Concepts
content: Before diving into the API, it helps to understand what's actually happening under the hood.

**Keys.** Every piece of saved data is identified by a key, just a string, like `"Gold"`, `"PlayerPosition"`, or `"Inventory"`. Think of a key as a filename. In fact, that's almost exactly what it becomes: by default, each key turns into its own `.json` file on disk, inside Unity's `Application.persistentDataPath`.
**The pipeline.** When you call `SetData`, your data goes through a small pipeline before it's written:

content.title: Save pipeline
code: your data -> serialize to JSON -> (optional) compress -> (optional) encrypt -> write

content: `GetData` runs the same pipeline in reverse:

content.title: Load pipeline
code: read -> (optional) decrypt -> (optional) decompress -> deserialize from JSON -> your data

content: You control the optional steps with parameters (`compress`, `encryptionKey`) covered later in this guide. The important thing to internalize now is the order: compression always happens before encryption, and decompression always happens after decryption. This matters because encrypted data looks like random noise, and random noise doesn't compress. So compressing first, while the data still has real structure, is the only order that makes sense.

**Serialization.** Unity's built-in `JsonUtility` does the actual JSON conversion. `JsonUtility` is fast and simple, but it has a few quirks. For example, it can't serialize a bare number or a `Dictionary` directly. Part of what this package does is quietly work around those quirks (via small wrapper/surrogate types) so you never have to think about them.

**Storage providers.** Where the final bytes actually end up is controlled by a `StorageProvider`, an object implementing the `ISaveStorage` interface. By default this is `LocalDiskStorage`, which writes to local disk. You can swap this out for your own backend (cloud save, a server, etc.) covered later in this guide.

content.content: With no slot specified, DeleteAll() deletes everything under Application.persistentDataPath, the entire save root, recursively. title: Complex Types
content: This is where the package earns its keep. `SetData`/`GetData` aren't limited to simple values, they understand a wide range of types natively.
**Unity math/geometry types.** `Vector2`, `Vector3`, `Vector4`, `Quaternion`, `Color`, `Rect`, `Bounds` all work directly:

Under the hood, `JsonUtility` can't serialize these types at the root of a JSON document on its own, so the package quietly converts them to and from small internal "surrogate" structs. You never see this and never have to worry about it, you just save and load the type you actually have.
**Dates.**
**Primitives, strings, enums.**
Same reasoning as above: `JsonUtility` can't serialize a bare `int`/`string`/`enum` at the root either, so these are automatically wrapped internally.
**Collections.** `List<T>`, arrays, 2D arrays, `Dictionary<K,V>`, `Stack<T>`, `Queue<T>`, `HashSet<T>`, and `LinkedList<T>` are all supported directly, pass the collection as-is:
`InventorySaverExample.cs` demonstrates saving a `List<InventoryItem>`. Notice the important detail on the item type itself:

content.title: [System.Serializable] is not optional
content.content: JsonUtility only serializes types explicitly marked with [System.Serializable]. Fields also need to be mutable (not readonly). JsonUtility writes loaded values directly into a type's fields, bypassing any constructor, and Unity's serializer skips readonly fields entirely. Skipping either of these will silently produce empty or missing data instead of an obvious error.

content: **Your own classes and structs.** Any plain class or struct marked `[System.Serializable]` works the same way. Just save it directly, no wrapping needed.
**GameObjects.** `GameObject` gets its own convenience overloads, since a `GameObject` isn't really "data" in the same sense as everything above:

Two important differences from everything else in this section: there is no `GetData<GameObject>()`, since a `GameObject` can't be conjured out of nothing, someone has to have created or found the instance first. So instead of loading a new one, `LoadInto` applies the saved state (name, active state, position, rotation, scale) onto an instance you already have. Calling `GetData<GameObject>()` directly will throw a clear exception telling you to use `LoadInto` instead, rather than failing silently.
`GameObjectSaver.cs` shows this pattern (using the async versions, covered later in this guide):

title: Save Slots
content: A slot is a named, isolated bucket for save data. Think "Slot 1 / Slot 2 / Slot 3" in a traditional save game menu, or separate save files per profile.

This is the key thing to understand: the same key means completely different data in different slots. `"PlayerData"` in `"Slot1"` and `"PlayerData"` in `"Slot2"` never collide. Internally, the slot becomes part of the file path, so each slot effectively gets its own folder. You reuse the same key names across every slot without worrying about them overwriting each other.
`Exists`, `Delete`, and `DeleteAll` all accept the same `slot` parameter, letting you scope any operation to one slot:
`CharacterSlotsExample.cs` puts this together into a slot-select flow: check if a slot has data, load it if so, or create a default entry if not.
If you never pass a `slot`, everything goes into one shared un-slotted space, which is exactly what most games with a single save file want.

title: Encryption
content: Encryption scrambles your save data so it can't be casually read or edited. Most useful for anything a player might be tempted to tamper with, like currency or unlock flags.

The package uses AES-256 (via `AESEncryption`, `System.Security.Cryptography.Aes` under the hood). Whatever string you pass as `encryptionKey` is hashed (SHA-256) into a proper 256-bit key, so it can be any length. A fresh random IV (initialization vector) is generated for every single save and stored alongside the ciphertext. This means saving the exact same value twice produces two different-looking encrypted results, which is intentional and is what makes the encryption actually secure.

content.title: The key must match exactly
content.content: Get it wrong, and you'll either get an exception (caught internally and logged) or garbled data back. There's no way to distinguish "wrong key" from "corrupted data" from the outside.

content.title: Don't hardcode a real key
content.content: Anyone can decompile a shipped build and read a plain hardcoded string straight out. AccountLogInExample.cs does exactly this for simplicity, but a real game should derive the key from something less obvious. Combining a build-time constant with a device identifier, for example.

content: Encryption can be freely combined with compression and slots. See the pipeline described in the Basic Concepts section.

title: Compression
content: Compression shrinks your save data. Worth turning on once a save gets large: an open-world state, a big inventory, anything with a lot of repeated structure.

content.title: Compress must match
content.content: Compress isn't auto-detected. You must pass the same value on load as you did on save. Loading with the wrong setting will throw, since it'll try to Gzip-decompress data that was never compressed (or vice versa).

content: You can combine compression with encryption:

As covered in Basic Concepts, compression always runs before encryption on save, and decryption always runs before decompression on load. You don't need to manage this order yourself, just pass both parameters and the pipeline handles it correctly.
`InventorySaverExample.cs` demonstrates compression on a `List<InventoryItem>`.

title: SaveAsync & LoadAsync
content: Every core method has an async counterpart:

The synchronous versions can briefly block the calling thread while data is written or read, usually negligible for small local saves, but noticeable for large saves, or for a custom storage provider that talks to the network. The async versions let your game keep running while the save/load happens in the background.

The default `LocalDiskStorage` implements a companion interface, `IAsyncSaveStorage`, doing genuine asynchronous file I/O (not just running the synchronous version on a background thread). If you write your own custom storage provider and it's naturally async, an HTTP call, for example, implement `IAsyncSaveStorage` on it too, and `SetDataAsync`/`GetDataAsync` will call your async methods directly instead of falling back to a background thread.

Following the same rule as the synchronous version: there's no `GetDataAsync<GameObject>()`, since a GameObject can't be created from nothing. Use `LoadIntoAsync` instead, applying the saved state onto an existing instance:

content.title: Awaiting inside OnDestroy
content.content: Awaiting inside OnDestroy is a little risky in general. If the object is being destroyed as part of a scene unload, the reference might not survive long enough for the await to resume cleanly. It's fine for a small example. In production code, prefer triggering saves from something more deterministic, like a "Save & Quit" button.

title: File Backups And Corruption Recovery
content: This feature is fully automatic, there's no API to call, no parameter to set. It's worth understanding anyway, since it affects what you'll see on disk.

**What happens on every save.** Before `LocalDiskStorage` (the default storage provider) overwrites a save file, it copies the previous version to a `.bak` file next to it. The new data is then written to a temporary file first, and only swapped into place once the write finishes completely. This means a crash or power loss mid-write can never leave you with a half-written, corrupt save file. You either get the old file or the fully-written new one, never something in between. Even if a save file somehow becomes unreadable later, the previous good version is still sitting right next to it.

**What happens on load.** If `GetData` (or the lower-level `StorageProvider.GetData`) can't read the primary file for any reason, it automatically falls back to the `.bak` file before giving up. This is transparent, you don't write any extra code to benefit from it.
**Manual recovery.** If you want to inspect or manually restore a backup, the in-editor Save Manager has a "Restore From Backup" button for exactly this.

title: Auto Save Manager Component
content: `AutoSaveManager` is a `MonoBehaviour` you place on any GameObject in your scene to handle ongoing, automatic saving, instead of calling `SetData` by hand every time something changes.
Add the component via Add Component -> Swimpie -> Simple Save & Load -> Auto Save Manager, or in code:

Inspector settings:

- **Save Mode** - `Interval`, `OnQuit`, or `IntervalAndOnQuit` - when automatic saves happen.
- **Interval** - seconds between saves (only editable/used if Save Mode includes Interval).
- **Slot** - which slot all registered entries save into.
- **Encryption Key** - optional, encrypts everything this manager saves.
- **Compress** - optional, compresses everything this manager saves.
- **Save On Pause** - also save when the app is paused, e.g. mobile home button (only editable/used if Save Mode includes OnQuit).
Nothing is auto-saved until you tell the manager about it, using `AddToAutoSave`. There are a few overloads depending on what you're registering.

content.title: Why Awake(), not Start()
content.content: Every AddToAutoSave call loads that entry's saved value immediately upon registration. Registering in Awake() means the value is already loaded before any Start() method elsewhere might expect it to be.

title: In-Editor Save Manager
content: A dedicated editor window for inspecting your save files without leaving Unity. Open it via Tools -> Swimpie -> Saves Manager.

What it lets you do:

- Browse every save file, optionally filtered by slot and by a key search string.
- Open the local save folder directly in your file explorer.
- Preview a save file's raw content.
- Decrypt / Decompress a preview on demand, enter the encryption key and/or toggle "Data is GZip Compressed" to view the real content of an encrypted or compressed save.
- Restore From Backup, manually overwrite a save file with its `.bak` copy.
- Delete individual save files, or use Delete ALL Saves to wipe everything for the currently-filtered slot.

content.title: Editor-only tool
content.content: This window is purely a development/debugging tool, it doesn't run in a build, and nothing you do here is required for your game to work correctly.
